sentences.text: Australosuchus clarkae is an extinct genus of crocodylian, with the species name honoring Elaine Clark. The name combines Latin and Greek roots to mean "southern crocodile." This animal possessed a moderately broad and flattened skull. The upper jaw held fourteen teeth on each side, while the lower jaw contained between sixteen and seventeen teeth. Researchers estimated its total length to be around three meters. A distinct feature was the vestigial fifth toe, which was robust and thicker than in other crocodilians.
Fossils of this animal were mentioned in scientific literature as early as 1968, decades before the genus was formally described.
It holds the record for the southernmost distribution of any mekosuchine, found only below 27°S latitude.

Willis and Molnar first described the genus in 1991 from fossil materials discovered at Lake Palankarinna in South Australia. The holotype specimen, catalogued as QM F16788, is a partial skeleton collected in 1975. It was found in the Etadunna Formation near Lake Palankarinna.
Researchers suggest Australosuchus was cold-resistant, allowing it to live in freshwater systems too cold for other crocodilians.
Due to the lack of specialized adaptations like ziphodont teeth or a longirostrine skull, it is thought to have been a generalized member of Mekosuchinae.
The genus belongs to the subfamily Mekosuchinae.

Australosuchus lived during the Late Oligocene and Early Miocene epochs. Australosuchus clarkae inhabited the Lake Eyre Basin in South Australia. Its fossil range spans from the Late Oligocene to the Early Miocene. It lived between 27.3 and 15.98 million years ago.
It is debated whether some fossils belong to the Mampuwordu Sands (Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene) or were reworked from older strata.
A 2021 morphological analysis by Rio and Mannion placed Australosuchus outside Mekosuchinae as the sister taxon to Crocodylidae.
Some phylogenetic analyses suggest Kalthifrons or a clade of Kalthifrons and Kambara might be more basal than Australosuchus.
